hero.headline: 6.1 magnitude earthquake off Cuba felt across Florida, prompts building evacuations in Miami
hero.teaser: A 6.1 magnitude earthquake off the west-northwest coast of Cuba Tuesday prompted evacuations of several buildings across Miami and was felt as far north as Jacksonville.
hero.body:
A 6.1 magnitude earthquake struck off the west-northwest coast of Cuba on Tuesday, sending tremors across Florida that were felt as far north as Jacksonville. The seismic activity triggered immediate building evacuations throughout the Miami area as residents and workers experienced the unexpected shaking. The quake's effects were significant enough to interrupt daily activities at multiple locations across the city, though the National Weather Service confirmed there was no tsunami risk from the earthquake and no injuries were reported.

The evacuation procedures at several Miami buildings caught many people off guard. Students at Fusion Academy were evacuated along with others in nearby structures. Maria Torrado, a student at the academy, described how those on higher floors experienced the earthquake more intensely than those lower down. She noted that the evacuation alarm sounded different from typical fire drills, with officials explicitly stating this was not a drill, which made the situation feel particularly alarming to students present.

Interestingly, not all employees and students in evacuated buildings actually felt the earthquake firsthand. At the Swatch Watchmaking School, staff and students were evacuated without initially understanding why. Jack Hodapp explained that while people in the break room sensed some type of earthquake and began evacuating, he and others nearby felt nothing at all. This confusion about whether the evacuation was necessary created some skepticism among those unaffected by the tremors. Streets surrounding the affected buildings were temporarily blocked off as the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office established a command center to manage the situation and coordinate response efforts. Within a short time, those who had been evacuated were allowed to return inside their buildings.

For some people caught in the evacuation, the confusion extended beyond not feeling the earthquake. Juan Cardona initially misinterpreted the crowded streets and blocked-off areas as signs of a criminal incident rather than a natural disaster. It was only after speaking with other people at the scene that he learned about the earthquake in Cuba and understood how it had impacted the Florida area. His experience reflects how the sudden nature of the evacuation and the general confusion left some unclear about what had actually occurred until they gathered more information from those around them.

cards.headline: 6.1 magnitude earthquake off Cuba felt in Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie, and across Treasure Coast
cards.teaser: A 6.1 magnitude earthquake struck Monday afternoon approximately 65 miles west of Mantua, Cuba, with tremors felt across the Treasure Coast including Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
A 6.1 magnitude earthquake confirmed by the U.S. Geological Survey struck just after 2 p.m. Monday approximately 65 miles west of Mantua, Cuba. The tremors were felt across much of Florida, from the Tampa Bay area to Miami-Dade County, prompting hundreds of residents to share firsthand accounts on social media. Carol Carsten in Port Saint Lucie said she was lying on a chaise lounge in her lanai and felt just the slightest of shaking. A WPTV viewer in Fort Pierce reported being on the 5th floor and feeling the floor sway. In Boynton Beach, Lynn Wollman described her whole building swaying for 5 to 7 seconds. The earthquake occurred at a relatively shallow depth of about 10 miles below the surface, which helped transmit the shaking across the water to Florida's coast.

The National Tsunami Warning Center confirmed there is no tsunami danger for the U.S. east coast, the Gulf of America states, or the eastern coast of Canada. Several buildings were evacuated as a precaution, including the Miami-Dade Government Center and Miami Beach City Hall. The National Weather Service in Miami confirmed reports of shaking from across southwestern Florida. No significant damage has been reported, and authorities continue to monitor the situation. No aftershocks have been reported and no damage has been documented in Florida.

cards.headline: 6.1 magnitude earthquake off Cuba felt across Treasure Coast from Vero Beach to Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A 6.1 magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Cuba Monday afternoon and was felt across Florida, including in West Palm Beach, Boynton Beach, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce, and as far north as Jacksonville.
cards.body:
A 6.1 magnitude earthquake struck just off the coast of Cuba around 2:15 p.m. Monday and was felt across Florida, with shaking reports reaching as far north as Jacksonville. Caleb Bennett and Jonathan Lisnoff were working on the 15th floor of the Northbridge Center off Flagler Drive in West Palm Beach when the quake hit. Bennett said he felt dizzy and the chains on the windows started slapping against the wall. Lisnoff, a Florida native, said the experience was unlike anything he had felt before.

Paul Earl, a seismologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, said the earthquake is historically significant for the region, calling it the largest earthquake in that immediate area on record. The quake did not occur on a plate boundary, where earthquakes typically originate, but rather on a fault within the plate due to built-up pressure. Earl said aftershocks are likely, though whether they will be felt is uncertain. The National Tsunami Warning Center said there is no tsunami danger for the U.S. east coast, the Gulf of America states, or the eastern coast of Canada. A 4.0 earthquake occurred off the coast of Florida northeast of Vero Beach in 2024 and was felt in Indian River County.

cards.headline: Former state Sen. Annette Taddeo enters Florida CFO race, challenges property tax overhaul and state spending priorities
cards.teaser: Annette Taddeo launched her campaign Monday for Florida chief financial officer, positioning herself as an independent watchdog against what she describes as un.
cards.body:
Annette Taddeo launched her campaign Monday for Florida chief financial officer, positioning herself as an independent watchdog against government spending. The South Florida Democrat is challenging Republican CFO Blaise Ingoglia, whom Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed to the position last summer. Taddeo said the statewide office has lacked proper checks and balances for nearly 30 years and criticized Ingoglia for not auditing costs at the Everglades immigration detention facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," which she said costs a million dollars daily. She argued the CFO should scrutinize state spending as much as local government expenditures, which Ingoglia has spent months auditing to identify wasteful spending.

Those local audits support the Republican case for a proposed property tax overhaul heading to voters in November that would expand the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Taddeo questioned whether lawmakers moved too quickly on the changes, warning the plan could shift costs rather than reduce them meaningfully. Before facing Ingoglia in the general election, Taddeo must compete for the Democratic nomination against Earle Ford, an attorney and former IRS employee who is emphasizing accountability and consumer protections. Ford has called the property tax debate a distraction from rising homeowners insurance costs. Candidate qualifying is underway this week, with the primary election scheduled for Aug. 18 and the general election in November.

cards.teaser: Annette Taddeo launched a campaign Monday for Florida chief financial officer, challenging Republican CFO Blaise Ingoglia in a race centered on government accou.
cards.body:
Annette Taddeo launched her campaign Monday for Florida chief financial officer, positioning herself as an independent watchdog for government spending and accountability. The South Florida Democrat is challenging Republican CFO Blaise Ingoglia, whom Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed to the position last summer. Taddeo criticized Ingoglia for not auditing costs at the Everglades immigration detention facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," saying the state spends a million dollars a day there. She also questioned whether lawmakers moved too quickly on a proposed property tax amendment heading to November voters that would expand the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Taddeo warned the plan could shift costs rather than meaningfully reduce them.

Before facing Ingoglia in the general election, Taddeo must compete for the Democratic nomination against Earle Ford, an attorney and former IRS employee. Ford is emphasizing accountability and consumer protections, arguing the state should prioritize rising homeowners insurance costs over property tax cuts. He is calling for stronger enforcement and greater transparency surrounding rate increases. Candidate qualifying is underway this week, with Florida's primary election scheduled for Aug. 18 and the general election set for November.

cards.headline: Mobile clinic brings prenatal care to Okeechobee mothers every Tuesday at public library
cards.teaser: Mom Mobile stations a 38-foot clinic at the Okeechobee public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday, offering maternity care to expecting mothers in a county with no delivery hospitals.
cards.body:
A mobile prenatal clinic is bringing maternity care directly to Okeechobee County, where no hospitals deliver babies and the nearest delivery hospitals are in Fort Pierce or Highlands County. The Mom Mobile program started with the Martin County Healthy Start Coalition and expanded to Okeechobee after Andrea Medellin with the Okeechobee Healthy Start Coalition saw its success. The 38-foot mobile clinic is stationed at the public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday, designed to offer care in a safe and welcoming environment.

The need for the service was evident immediately. Fifteen women were seen during the first three days of operation, and appointment requests continue to grow. Medellin said the visits are intentional and specifically designed to serve quality care for high-risk and high-need mothers rather than rushing through appointments. Twenty-year-old Evelyn Allen, who lives in rural Martin County, struggled to find affordable prenatal resources before discovering Mom Mobile. She initially was terrified when she learned she was pregnant but found the program to be a blessing, calling it lucky to have access to the clinic's support and services.

cards.headline: Jupiter bar DAS Beer Garden plans World Cup street party, free beer for Team USA goals
cards.teaser: DAS Beer Garden in Jupiter is preparing for the FIFA World Cup with free beer for every Team USA goal and a street party on Town Center Drive for the final match.
cards.body:
DAS Beer Garden in Jupiter is preparing for the FIFA World Cup with special promotions including free beer for every Team USA goal and a street party planned for the final match. Co-owner Alex Marquez said the World Cup brings an energy unlike any other sporting event. "When the World Cup starts, it's just different. You can just see the vibe changes, everybody gets really into it," Marquez said. He noted that the tournament carries deeper meaning for fans than typical matches. "Now it's your country. It's your blood, it's your heritage," Marquez said. He added that soccer's lower-scoring nature makes goals more impactful, creating electric moments when they occur.

Soccer fan Jason Pitman plans to attend DAS Beer Garden's World Cup watch parties, including morning events where he said he will be "one of those people at 9 a.m. eating those donuts that Alex brings in." Pitman expressed optimism about Team USA's chances. "I think we're talented. I think it's just a matter of trying to put that talent together," Pitman said. He predicted the atmosphere during big matches will be memorable. "The big games are going to be bananas," Pitman said. For the World Cup Final, DAS Beer Garden plans to shut down Town Center Drive and set up a big screen television across the street for an outdoor soccer street party. The tavern is located at 1203 Town Center Dr 116 in Jupiter.

cards.headline: Jupiter and Venus make closest approach tonight in rare alignment visible after sunset
cards.teaser: Jupiter and Venus will make their closest approach tonight in the twilight sky, appearing about 1.5 degrees apart in what is sometimes called a cosmic kiss.
cards.body:
Two of the brightest planets will make their closest approach tonight in the twilight sky. Jupiter and Venus have been creeping closer and closer and will cross paths this evening. Head outside and look west northwest in the sky if it is clear enough to see Jupiter and Venus meet in what is sometimes referred to as a "cosmic kiss." Just after the 8:14 p.m. sunset, Venus will appear followed by Jupiter, which is not as bright. The pair will make their closest approach about 1.5 degrees apart, or as wide as your pinky held at arm's distance. Mercury will also appear low on the horizon.

The planets will set before 11 p.m., so make sure to check it out before then. After tonight, Venus will surpass Jupiter and appear farther west in the sky.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County implements 45-day anchoring limit in Indian River Lagoon and Fort Pierce Harbor
hero.teaser: New restrictions took effect June 1 in anchor limitation areas near the South Causeway Bridge to combat abandoned vessels and protect water quality.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County launched new anchoring restrictions on June 1 to address growing concerns about abandoned vessels in local waterways. The county established two anchor limitation areas in the Indian River Lagoon and Fort Pierce Harbor near the South Causeway Bridge. Under these new rules, boaters cannot anchor their vessels for more than 45 consecutive days within any six-month period in the designated areas. If boaters wish to anchor again after reaching this limit, they must leave all anchoring limitation areas for at least 24 hours before returning.

The county implemented these restrictions in response to an increasing number of derelict vessels appearing in the waterways. According to Erick Gill with St. Lucie County, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission collected approximately two dozen abandoned vessels in the area last year. These discarded boats create multiple problems for the region's water quality and navigation. James Beams with St. Lucie County Port, Inlet and Beaches explained that long-abandoned vessels pose environmental hazards, particularly from diesel and oil tanks and holding tanks that can contaminate the water.

Gill emphasized that the new anchoring restrictions serve multiple purposes for the community. The limitations will help keep the waterways clear and navigable, ensuring that vessels can move freely through these important passages. By reducing the number of abandoned vessels remaining in the water, the county aims to prevent pollutants from entering the lagoon ecosystem. Gill noted the ecological significance of protecting these waters, stating that "there's over 4,000 species of animals and plants and birds that live in the lagoon."

The restrictions represent St. Lucie County's effort to balance recreational boating access with environmental protection and waterway maintenance. By limiting how long vessels can remain anchored without interruption, the county hopes to discourage the abandonment of boats while still allowing legitimate anchoring for temporary purposes. Boaters who plan to stay in the anchoring limitation areas for extended periods will need to plan breaks from the waterways or relocate their vessels. St. Lucie County residents and visitors can find a detailed site map of the anchor limitation areas to help them understand where these new rules apply.

cards.headline: Florida property tax referendum could face up to five constitutional challenges before November vote
cards.teaser: Former state senator Jeff Brandes says the referendum to raise homestead exemptions to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028 may face legal challenges on multiple fronts.
cards.body:
The Florida property tax referendum could face up to five constitutional challenges before voters decide its fate on Election Day in November, according to former state Sen. Jeff Brandes. In a Saturday social media post, Brandes outlined potential legal challenges including Ballot Language, Equal Protection, Uniformity, Home Rule and Unfunded Mandates. "I think there's questions about home rule. Think there's questions about unfunded mandates. I think there's questions about taxing uniformity. There's a variety of questions," Brandes told WPTV on Monday.

State Rep. Toby Overdorf, R-Stuart, emphasized the significance of the measure after it was approved in special session last week. "We need to first of all remember this is not a normal bill. This is a joint resolution that changes the Constitution," Overdorf told WPTV. While Overdorf expects legal challenges, multiple lawsuits could strain the courts ahead of the November vote. Brandes said courts will need to consolidate the challenges and address key constitutional questions. The referendum would raise the homestead exemption for homeowners to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. No lawsuits have been filed against the referendum yet, but legal challenges are anticipated once the final ballot language is completed.

cards.headline: Florida property tax referendum faces five potential constitutional challenges

In a Saturday social media post, Brandes identified five possible legal challenges: ballot language, equal protection, uniformity, home rule, and unfunded mandates. "They're going to have to consolidate these things down," Brandes said. "There's probably a handful of really interesting questions that have to be asked and addressed." No lawsuits have been filed against the referendum at this point, though many expect them once the actual ballot language is completed.

cards.headline: Mom Mobile brings prenatal care to Okeechobee County and rural Martin County
cards.teaser: A mobile clinic called Mom Mobile is bringing prenatal care directly to expecting mothers in Okeechobee County and rural Martin County, where access to maternity services is limited.
cards.body:
Okeechobee County has no hospital that delivers babies, forcing many pregnant women to travel to Fort Pierce or Highlands County for care depending on where they live. The Mom Mobile program, which started with the Martin County Healthy Start Coalition, has expanded to address this gap by bringing prenatal care directly to expecting mothers in both counties. The 38-foot mobile clinic is stationed at the Okeechobee public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday, offering a safe and welcoming environment for care.

Andrea Medellin with the Okeechobee Healthy Start Coalition said the program's demand was immediately apparent. Fifteen women were seen during the first three days of operation, with appointment requests continuing to grow. The bus is designed for hour-long visits specifically to prioritize quality care for high-risk and high-need mothers rather than serving more patients. Twenty-year-old Evelyn Allen, who lives in rural Martin County, struggled to find affordable resources before discovering Mom Mobile. She said she could not find any resources, and those available required out-of-pocket payment. Allen called the program a blessing.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Commissioner Sara Baxter drops reelection bid to run for Congress
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County District 6 Commissioner Sara Baxter announced Monday she will run for Congress in the newly drawn District 22, leaving the western Palm Beach County commission seat open.
cards.body:
Palm Beach County Mayor and District 6 Commissioner Sara Baxter announced Monday that she will run for Congress in Florida's newly drawn District 22 seat, requiring her to drop out of the county commission race. Baxter, who was elected to the District 6 seat in 2022, represents western Palm Beach County including Royal Palm Beach, Loxahatchee Groves, Acreage, Wellington, Westlake, Belle Glade, South Bay, Pahokee, and West Lake Worth. Before her 2022 election, the self-proclaimed political outsider held no political office and previously ran a small business with her husband, Brian.

President Donald Trump has endorsed Baxter in her congressional bid, calling her "A true MAGA Warrior" and highlighting her work to grow the economy, promote American-made products, cut taxes and regulations, advance American energy dominance, stop migrant crime, support military and veterans, and defend Second Amendment rights. Baxter's departure opens the District 6 county commission seat to new candidates. Congressional District 22 is expected to be among South Florida's closely watched races in the 2026 election cycle. Candidate qualifying remains open, and additional candidates are anticipated to enter both races.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Golf Club renovation 50% complete, reopening set for November
cards.teaser: The $30 million renovation of Delray Beach Golf Club is already 50% complete as of early June, and city officials say the project remains on track to finish by the end of 2026.
cards.body:
The Delray Beach Golf Club has been closed since November 2025 for a $30 million makeover designed to restore its historic character while giving it a modern upgrade. City officials say the project is already 50% complete as of early June, and they're on track to finish by the end of 2026. The original course was designed by legendary architects Donald Ross and Dick Wilson, and the city is working to preserve those historic elements. The renovation is happening in phases, with the north 9 holes, called the Wilson 9, already fully grassed and growing in, while the south 9 holes, the Ross 9, are currently being grassed.

Ronnie Dunayer, a golf instructor who has taught at the course for 20 years, got a sneak peek at the progress recently and said it is looking better than anticipated. "So excited about what's happened and the opportunity to come back and play a virtually new golf course, but yet have the old integrity," Dunayer said. Not everyone is thrilled about the changes. Delray Beach resident Maureen Allyn said crews are opening large planting holes for trees near her home that could end up blocking her view of the golf course, and she is concerned the change could negatively impact her property's value. The city says the $30 million budget has not changed since work began, and they're still targeting a November 2026 reopening date.

cards.headline: Brightline and Tri-Rail offer cheaper transit options to World Cup matches at Hard Rock Stadium
cards.teaser: Transit options like Brightline and Tri-Rail could save World Cup fans significant money compared to driving and parking at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, where some parking passes cost $200.
cards.body:
Hard Rock Stadium will host seven World Cup matches beginning Monday, June 15, when Saudi Arabia plays Uruguay at 6 p.m. The final Miami match, the third-place game, is scheduled for Saturday, July 18 at 5 p.m. Brightline is the official transit partner for the FIFA World Cup 2026 in Miami, offering round-trip tickets ranging from $76 to $150. From the Brightline Aventura Station, Miami-Dade County will provide free Game Day Express shuttle buses directly to the stadium gates. These shuttles operate on a first-come, first-served basis, and riders must present a valid World Cup match ticket for that specific day to board.

Tri-Rail presents a more affordable option, with one-way tickets ranging from $2.50 to $6.90 depending on the starting station, and weekend round-trip travel available for $5. Both transit services cost significantly less than driving, as parking passes for Hard Rock Stadium must be purchased in advance and can cost as much as $200. Additional transportation options include Metrorail or Metrobus connections via the Miami-Dade Golden Glades Interchange to Metrobus Route 297 Orange Express, or rideshare services like Uber and Lyft at designated zones, though surge pricing and longer wait times are expected after matches.

hero.headline: West Palm Beach soccer fan heads to Miami for Cape Verde's historic World Cup debut
hero.body:
A West Palm Beach resident is traveling to Miami this month to witness Cape Verde's first-ever World Cup appearance. Eridjon Dacruz grew up in the island nation, an archipelago of 10 islands located off the African coast with a population of roughly half a million people, before relocating to the United States. The team, nicknamed the Tubarão Azul or Blue Sharks, has qualified for the World Cup tournament for the first time in the country's history. As Dacruz looked through his closet at his collection of national team jerseys, he reflected on what this achievement means for his home country, which gained independence from Portugal in the 1970s.

The qualification has sparked enormous celebration throughout Cape Verde. Dacruz, who still has many family members living on the islands, says the World Cup achievement has dominated conversations there. He recalls how difficult it once was to find Cape Verdean players represented in soccer video games, with only a handful appearing in the games he played growing up. His girlfriend surprised him with an unforgettable anniversary gift: a handwritten note inside a box that read "I'm going to the World Cup." Dacruz will attend Cape Verde's matchup against Uruguay in Miami, making the gift even more meaningful. He is currently waiting to receive the newest Cape Verde national jersey to wear to the game.

Cape Verde will open the tournament against Spain, one of the competition's top contenders. Despite facing strong opposition, Dacruz remains optimistic about his team's prospects. He believes that winning a couple of games could allow Cape Verde to advance further in the tournament than many might expect. The World Cup qualification carries significant financial benefits for the nation. Making the tournament will provide Cape Verde's soccer federation with more than 10 million dollars to invest in developing future generations of players.

Cape Verde's location near Africa means the islands frequently appear in weather discussions during hurricane season. Tropical systems often develop in the region before moving westward across the Atlantic toward the United States. Meteorologist Sami Squires explained that weather patterns originating near Cape Verde are tracked throughout hurricane season as they travel across the Atlantic, with forecasters monitoring their potential path toward the U.S. coast. For Dacruz, however, the islands represent something far more personal and meaningful than weather systems: they are his childhood home and the birthplace of a national team achieving what once seemed impossible.

cards.headline: Mobile clinic brings prenatal care to Okeechobee mothers every Tuesday at public library
cards.teaser: Mom Mobile stations a 38-foot clinic at the Okeechobee public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday, offering maternity care to expecting mothers in a county with no delivery hospitals.
cards.body:
A mobile prenatal clinic is bringing maternity care directly to Okeechobee County, where no hospitals deliver babies and the nearest delivery hospitals are in Fort Pierce or Highlands County. The Mom Mobile program started with the Martin County Healthy Start Coalition and expanded to Okeechobee after Andrea Medellin with the Okeechobee Healthy Start Coalition saw its success. The 38-foot mobile clinic is stationed at the public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday, designed to offer care in a safe and welcoming environment.

The need for the service was evident immediately. Fifteen women were seen during the first three days of operation, and appointment requests continue to grow. Medellin said the visits are intentional and specifically designed to serve quality care for high-risk and high-need mothers rather than rushing through appointments. Twenty-year-old Evelyn Allen, who lives in rural Martin County, struggled to find affordable prenatal resources before discovering Mom Mobile. She initially was terrified when she learned she was pregnant but found the program to be a blessing, calling it lucky to have access to the clinic's support and services.

cards.headline: 6.1 magnitude earthquake off Cuba felt across Treasure Coast from Vero Beach to Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A 6.1 magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Cuba Monday afternoon and was felt across Florida, including in West Palm Beach, Boynton Beach, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce, and as far north as Jacksonville.
cards.body:
A 6.1 magnitude earthquake struck just off the coast of Cuba around 2:15 p.m. Monday and was felt across Florida, with shaking reports reaching as far north as Jacksonville. Caleb Bennett and Jonathan Lisnoff were working on the 15th floor of the Northbridge Center off Flagler Drive in West Palm Beach when the quake hit. Bennett said he felt dizzy and the chains on the windows started slapping against the wall. Lisnoff, a Florida native, said the experience was unlike anything he had felt before.

Paul Earl, a seismologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, said the earthquake is historically significant for the region, calling it the largest earthquake in that immediate area on record. The quake did not occur on a plate boundary, where earthquakes typically originate, but rather on a fault within the plate due to built-up pressure. Earl said aftershocks are likely, though whether they will be felt is uncertain. The National Tsunami Warning Center said there is no tsunami danger for the U.S. east coast, the Gulf of America states, or the eastern coast of Canada. A 4.0 earthquake occurred off the coast of Florida northeast of Vero Beach in 2024 and was felt in Indian River County.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie resident felt earthquake swaying on chaise lounge during Cuba quake
cards.teaser: Carol Carsten in Port St. Lucie said she felt slight shaking while lying on a chaise lounge in her lanai during the 6.1 magnitude earthquake that struck off Cuba Monday.
cards.body:
Hundreds of Floridians took to social media Monday afternoon to describe the unusual shaking they felt as a 6.1 magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Cuba. The U.S. Geological Survey confirmed the earthquake occurred just after 2 p.m. approximately 65 miles west of Mantua, Cuba at a shallow depth of about 10 miles below the surface. The tremors were felt across much of Florida, from the Tampa Bay area down to Miami-Dade County. Carol Carsten in Port Saint Lucie said she was lying on a chaise lounge in her lanai and felt just the slightest of shaking. A WPTV viewer on the fifth floor in Fort Pierce said they could actually feel the floor swaying.

Lynn Wollman in Boynton Beach reported that the whole building was swaying for a good 5 to 7 seconds. Erica Smith Chepurko in North Palm Beach said her TV and computer monitor shook on the fourth floor of her office building. Daniela Maquer in Boca Raton experienced swaying and vibrating and said it reminded her of past earthquakes in Venezuela. The National Weather Service in Miami confirmed reports of shaking from across southwestern Florida. The National Tsunami Warning Center assured residents there is no tsunami danger for the U.S. east coast or Gulf of America states. Several buildings were evacuated as a precaution, including the Miami-Dade Government Center and Miami Beach City Hall. No significant damage has been reported and no aftershocks have been documented in Florida.

cards.headline: Miami buildings evacuated as 6.1 earthquake tremors reach Jacksonville
cards.teaser: A 6.1 magnitude earthquake off Cuba prompted evacuations of several buildings across Miami on Tuesday, with shaking felt as far north as Jacksonville.
cards.body:
A 6.1 magnitude earthquake off the west-northwest coast of Cuba prompted evacuations of several buildings across Miami on Tuesday and was felt as far north as Jacksonville. Students at Fusion Academy were among those evacuated when their building shook. Student Maria Torrado said people on the top floors felt the shaking more intensely than those on lower levels. She described the evacuation alarm as different from a typical fire drill, with announcements saying "this is not a drill" and ordering immediate evacuation.

Not all employees felt the tremor. Students at the Swatch Watchmaking School were evacuated but initially had no idea why. Jack Hodapp said others in the break room felt what they believed was an earthquake, but his group did not feel anything at first. Streets near some affected buildings were blocked off as the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office set up a command center. Those evacuated were let back inside shortly after. Juan Cardona, who was present during the evacuation, initially thought there was a criminal scene before learning from others that an earthquake in Cuba had impacted the Florida area. The National Weather Service said there is no tsunami risk as a result of the quake, and no injuries have been reported.

cards.headline: Delray Beach Golf Club renovation 50% complete, on track for November reopening
cards.teaser: The $30 million renovation of Delray Beach Golf Club is halfway done as of early June and remains on track for completion by the end of 2026, city officials say.
cards.body:
Delray Beach Golf Club's $30 million renovation is progressing on schedule, with the project 50% complete as of early June. The course has been closed since November 2025 for the makeover, which aims to restore its historic character while modernizing the facility. City officials say they remain on track to finish by the end of 2026, with a November 2026 reopening targeted.

The renovation is happening in phases to preserve the course's original design by legendary architects Donald Ross and Dick Wilson. The north nine holes, called the Wilson 9, are already fully grassed and growing in, while the south nine holes, the Ross 9, are currently being grassed. Ronnie Dunayer, a golf instructor who has taught at the course for 20 years, said the progress exceeded her expectations during a recent sneak peek. "I've been an advocate for improvement for a long time, and in all honesty, it's looking better than anticipated," Dunayer said. However, some residents have concerns about the project. Delray Beach resident Maureen Allyn contacted WPTV about planting holes being opened for trees near her home that could block her view of the golf course and potentially impact her property's value. The city says the $30 million budget has not changed since work began.

cards.headline: Rural Martin County woman finds prenatal care support through Mom Mobile program
cards.teaser: Evelyn Allen, a 20-year-old expecting mother living in rural Martin County, found prenatal care and support through the Mom Mobile program after struggling to find affordable resources.
cards.body:
Evelyn Allen was terrified when she first learned she was pregnant at age 20, just as she was getting her life back on track. Looking for support in rural Martin County, where options are limited, Allen struggled to find resources that didn't require out-of-pocket costs or unrealistic expectations. She discovered Mom Mobile, a maternity care program that started with the Martin County Healthy Start Coalition. The 38-foot mobile clinic brings prenatal care and support directly to expecting mothers and their families in a safe and welcoming environment.

The program has expanded to Okeechobee, where it addresses a critical gap in care. Okeechobee has no delivery hospitals, forcing expectant mothers to travel to Fort Pierce or Highlands County for delivery. The mobile clinic is stationed at the public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday. During the first three days of operation, 15 women were seen, with appointment requests continuing to grow. A nurse with the Okeechobee Healthy Start Coalition assured Allen that she can call anytime for support. Allen calls Mom Mobile a blessing, saying she has gotten really lucky with the program and its quality-focused approach to serving high-risk and vulnerable mothers.

hero.headline: Cornell Art Museum in Delray Beach opens 'Persistence of Matter' exhibit featuring upcycled art
hero.teaser: The Cornell Art Museum at Old School Square has opened its newest summer exhibition, Persistence of Matter, spotlighting artists who turn discarded materials into striking works of art.
hero.body:
Guest curators Mavis Benson and Pamela Lambie have selected artists whose sculptures, installations, and mixed media pieces are all crafted from reclaimed objects. Featured creators include Autumn Kioti, whose work draws on natural and urban influences, and Mike Silverman, whose Self-Reflection series uses discarded hard drive platters and printed circuit boards to create reflective sculptures. Every piece invites viewers to see themselves and their relationship to technology and waste in a new light, Silverman said.

The exhibition runs through Sept. 10, 2026, with special programs including artist talks, salon discussions, and film screenings. Museum hours are Wednesday from noon to 5 p.m., Thursday and Friday from noon to 7 p.m., Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and Sunday from noon to 5 p.m.

According to Delray Beach Downtown Development Authority Cultural Arts Director Marusca Gatto, the show underscores the museums mission to marry creativity with community impact. For event details, call 561-654-2220.

cards.headline: 'Beetlejuice' musical runs through June 7 at Kravis Center in West Palm Beach
cards.teaser: From wigs gone rogue to audience laughter echoing through the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall, 'Beetlejuice' the musical has landed at the Kravis Center.
cards.body:
Running June 2 through June 7 at the Kravis Center, "Beetlejuice" the musical brings its spooky humor, over-the-top visuals, and heartwarming moments to Palm Beach County. Actor Ryan Stajmiger steps into the iconic striped suit to play the mischievous demon from Tim Burton's 1988 film. "I've loved the movie since I was a kid. I'm a huge Tim Burton fan, and you know, Michael Keaton's performance is so iconic," Stajmiger told WPTV's T.A. "He's only in the movie for 15 minutes, but it's like lasted forever."

The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a "strange and unusual" teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble. Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts is laughing with the audience. "I get to break the fourth wall a lot, so I get to communicate directly to the audience and share some moments with them. That's my favorite part of theater," he explained. Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach to host finish line for 80-mile ocean paddle benefiting cystic fibrosis families
cards.body:
More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of the open Atlantic Ocean this June as part of the annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis. Event founder Travis Suit will lead participants launching from Bimini, Bahamas, at midnight on June 13, with paddlers arriving at Lake Worth Beach after 12 to 16 hours on the water. The endurance event benefits the Piper's Angels Foundation, which Suit established to honor his daughter Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4. The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10, featuring arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove, a 4Ocean beach cleanup and community buffet dinner on Thursday, and a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony on Friday to honor cystic fibrosis warriors.

Safety requirements are strict. All paddlers must wear U.S. Coast Guard-approved personal flotation devices, waterproof whistles, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by organizers must be worn and kept active throughout the crossing, and mandatory safety meetings will be held before launch. Fundraising minimums require paddlers to raise at least $2,000, while crew members and virtual participants must contribute a minimum of $500, with all donations due by July 31. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 for a daylong celebration welcoming the arriving paddlers. More information and registration details are available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

hero.headline: Gov. DeSantis endorses Wilton Simpson for second term as Florida Agriculture Commissioner
hero.teaser: Ron DeSantis endorsed Wilton Simpson for a second term as head of the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services. DeSantis credited Simpson with rejuvenating an agency and responding admirably to natural disasters including this year's fires.
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis has endorsed Wilton Simpson's reelection bid for Florida Agriculture Commissioner. DeSantis said Simpson has earned a second term since taking office in 2023, crediting him with turning around an agency that had struggled under previous leadership. The governor highlighted Simpson's response to natural disasters, including this year's wildfires, as evidence of his effectiveness in the role. President Donald Trump also backs Simpson's candidacy for a second term.

Simpson, an egg farmer from Trilby who previously served as state Senate President, was first elected agriculture commissioner in 2022. He has pursued legislative reform measures during his tenure, most notably the Florida Farm Bill passed during this legislative session. Simpson promoted the bill as protecting Floridians from dangerous and disruptive technologies, organized fraud, and government overreach. The legislation accomplished multiple goals, including preventing local governments from banning gasoline-powered equipment, establishing guardrails on development, expanding agritourism opportunities, creating the Florida Native Seed Research and Marketing Program, and making permanent the Farmers Feeding Florida Program.

Simpson maintains a substantial financial advantage over his opponents. His main political committee, Friends of Wilton Simpson, has more than 10 million dollars in the bank and raised 1.375 million dollars during the first three months of 2024. Simpson also chairs multiple other committees with significant resources, including the Florida Green PAC with nearly 11 million dollars on hand, the Future Florida political committee with nearly 12 million dollars, and the Home Grown PAC with more than 300,000 dollars. The other Republican candidates have far less financial backing. Matt the Welder of Plant City reported less than 40,000 dollars on hand, while Richard Olle of Valrico had not reported any fundraising as of the March reporting deadline.

Democrats Donald Prichard and Chase Anderson Romagnano have also opened campaign accounts, along with no-party candidate Kyle Gibson. Neither Democrat had raised funds as of the first quarter filing deadline, with Gibson reporting approximately 1,000 dollars on hand. DeSantis joins a growing list of endorsers backing Simpson's reelection. As of Wednesday morning, none of the candidates had officially qualified for the race, though filing deadlines were approaching.

cards.headline: Rep. Byron Donalds officially qualifies for Florida gubernatorial race
cards.teaser: Byron Donalds has officially qualified to run in Florida's 2026 gubernatorial race by paying the required fee. He is one of 10 candidates who had officially qualified as of Tuesday morning.
cards.body:
Rep. Byron Donalds officially qualified to run in Florida's 2026 gubernatorial race by paying the $8,484 fee required for party-affiliated candidates, which represents 6% of the gubernatorial salary. The qualifying period opened Monday and runs through Friday. According to the Florida Division of Elections website, 10 candidates had officially qualified as of Tuesday morning, including five Republicans, two Democrats, two NPAs, and a write-in candidate. Other leading GOP candidates who have qualified include former House Speaker Paul Renner, hedge fund manager James Fishback, and pastor Bobby Williams.

Donalds has secured President Trump's "complete and total endorsement," which he received in February 2025. According to recent polls, he leads his Republican primary opponents significantly. David Jolly, the presumptive Democratic nominee after Orange County Mayor Jerry Demings withdrew to focus on his prostate cancer treatment, has not yet qualified. Poll aggregates show Donalds leading Jolly by single digits, though the most recent survey gave Jolly a four-point lead. Both Sabato's Crystal Ball and the Cook Political Report rate the race as Safe Republican and Solid Republican, respectively. Donalds' campaign has raised $81 million from 35,000 donors and reported knocking on 72,400 doors across the state.

cards.headline: Former state Sen. Annette Taddeo enters Florida CFO race, challenges property tax overhaul and state spending priorities
cards.teaser: Annette Taddeo launched her campaign Monday for Florida chief financial officer, positioning herself as an independent watchdog against what she describes as un.
cards.body:
Annette Taddeo launched her campaign Monday for Florida chief financial officer, positioning herself as an independent watchdog against government spending. The South Florida Democrat is challenging Republican CFO Blaise Ingoglia, whom Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed to the position last summer. Taddeo said the statewide office has lacked proper checks and balances for nearly 30 years and criticized Ingoglia for not auditing costs at the Everglades immigration detention facility known as "Alligator Alcatraz," which she said costs a million dollars daily. She argued the CFO should scrutinize state spending as much as local government expenditures, which Ingoglia has spent months auditing to identify wasteful spending.

Those local audits support the Republican case for a proposed property tax overhaul heading to voters in November that would expand the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. Taddeo questioned whether lawmakers moved too quickly on the changes, warning the plan could shift costs rather than reduce them meaningfully. Before facing Ingoglia in the general election, Taddeo must compete for the Democratic nomination against Earle Ford, an attorney and former IRS employee who is emphasizing accountability and consumer protections. Ford has called the property tax debate a distraction from rising homeowners insurance costs. Candidate qualifying is underway this week, with the primary election scheduled for Aug. 18 and the general election in November.

cards.headline: Gov. DeSantis signs local bills changing Jacksonville Aviation Authority, Duval Schools, and Nassau County government
cards.teaser: Ron DeSantis approved three local bills that will change government in Northeast Florida. The bills affect the Jacksonville Aviation Authority, Duval County School Board, and Nassau County recreation districts.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis has signed three local bills that will modify government structures in Northeast Florida. House Speaker Pro Tempore Wyman Duggan carried two measures impacting Duval County in the House, while Rep. Dean Black sponsored legislation for Nassau County. Clay Yarborough served as the Senate sponsor for all three bills.

HB 4045, one of Duggan's bills, changes local charter and directs the Jacksonville Aviation Authority to ensure Cecil Airport develops and expands as a spaceport. The measure establishes an Economic Development Committee tasked with bringing direct route international flights to Jacksonville International Airport and driving more aerospace business to Cecil Field, with annual reporting required. HB 4049, Duggan's second bill, grants the Duval County School Board internal counsel, though the School Board lawyer remains subject to Jacksonville's General Counsel's binding opinion. During the legislative process, Jacksonville City Council members opposed granting the School Board lawyer greater autonomy beyond what the Charter contemplates. Black's HB 4017 terminates Nassau County Recreation Water Conservation Control Districts established in the 1960s through special legislative act. Though only one district is affected and it has been dormant for 23 years, the removal will transfer all assets and liabilities to the Nassau County Board of County Commissioners and reduce administrative costs.

cards.headline: FloridaCommerce opens grant applications for military communities until July 7
cards.teaser: Applications are now being accepted for Defense Reinvestment and Florida Defense Support Commission grant programs designed to benefit military communities with bases and installations. The application period runs until July 7.
cards.body:
FloridaCommerce is accepting applications for Defense Reinvestment Grant and Florida Defense Support Commission grant programs until July 7. The programs target defense-dependent municipal governments and economic development panels with military installations in their areas. Secretary of Commerce J. Alex Kelly said the grant cycle continues Gov. Ron DeSantis' mission to ensure Florida remains the most military and veteran-friendly state in the nation. Since 2019, more than $40 million has been invested into Florida's military communities through Florida's military and defense grant programs, strengthening critical infrastructure and bolstering workforce readiness. FloridaCommerce has streamlined the application process, allowing all entities to email applications to [email protected]. Funding distribution is contingent on the state budget.

DRG funding supports community-based activities that provide community investment and job creation, including reuse of closed or realigned military facilities. The Economic Development Commission of Florida's Space Coast created wastewater treatment studies and implemented communications plans. Florida's Great Northwest economic development agency funded an analysis of transitioning veterans into the workforce and created information resources. FDSC funds provide community protection around military installations. Jacksonville implemented protections near Naval Air Station Jacksonville and Naval Station Mayport entrances. Polk County acquired conservation land easements near Avon Park Air Force Range. The University of West Florida used FDSC funding to help students prepare for security clearances when applying for Florida-based defense contracting companies.

cards.headline: Former Tampa Mayor Bob Buckhorn raises $215,000 for 2027 mayoral bid, maintains nearly $2 million on hand
cards.teaser: Former Tampa Mayor Bob Buckhorn's political committee raised $215,370 from April 1 through May 31, bringing his total raised to more than $2 million. He maintains nearly $2 million on hand for his bid to become Mayor again.
cards.body:
Former Tampa Mayor Bob Buckhorn's political committee, Friends of Bob Buckhorn, raised $215,370 from April 1 through May 31, bringing his total to $2.05 million with nearly $2 million remaining on hand. Major contributors during the recent period included $30,000 from Cigar City PC run by Democratic compliance expert Jonathan Brill, $25,000 each from McCormick Drive LLC run by Ronald Wanek of Ashley Furniture and The Yerrid Law Firm, and $20,000 from automotive sales executive Preston Farrior. The committee also received $10,000 each from KETTLER President of Development James Nozar, Central 120 LLC, Bridgeview Holdings, accountant Frank Scalfaro, and restaurateurs Kyle and Chas Bruck.

Most recent expenses went to Washington D.C.-based Hamburger Group Creative for $15,000 in media content and production, with $5,000 to GW Strategies in Miami Shores for fundraising and over $2,600 reimbursing Buckhorn for event costs. Buckhorn's primary opposition likely comes from Tampa City Council member Bill Carlson, who entered the race two days after Buckhorn filed in April. As of March 31, Carlson's political committee had raised just over $34,000. A dark money organization, Leading Tampa Inc., launched in March to support Carlson. The mayoral election is scheduled for March 2, 2027, with a runoff on April 27, 2027, if no candidate receives more than 50 percent of the vote.

cards.headline: Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd endorses Sydney Gruters for Congress, completing sweep of CD 16 sheriffs
cards.teaser: Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd endorsed Sydney Gruters for Congress, making her six for six with endorsements from every sheriff in the six counties spanning Florida's 16th Congressional District.
cards.body:
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd endorsed Sydney Gruters for Congress, completing the sweep of all six sheriffs in Florida's 16th Congressional District. Judd said Gruters is "the real deal" and understands that public safety means backing law enforcement officers, getting tough on criminals and ensuring law-abiding families can live in peace. He noted that President Trump trusts Gruters, and so does he. Prior endorsements from the other five sheriffs in the district include Hardee County Sheriff Vent Crawford, Pinellas County Sheriff Bob Gualtieri, Sarasota County Sheriff Kurt Hoffman, DeSoto County Sheriff Jim Potter and Manatee County Sheriff Rick Wells.

Gruters, a former New College Foundation leader who previously worked for the Department of Agriculture and for U.S. Representatives Vern Buchanan and Greg Steube, said she was honored by Judd's support. She pledged to back law enforcement, fight to secure the border and work with law enforcement to keep communities safe. The Suncoast Professional Firefighters and Paramedics, St. Petersburg Firefighters and Hardee County Firefighters also endorsed Gruters. Gruters spokesperson Max Goodman said the most respected public safety leaders in Florida and the district are supporting her because she is serious, honest and ready to do the job.

hero.headline: Mom Mobile brings prenatal care to rural Martin County expecting mothers
hero.body:
A mobile prenatal clinic program is now serving expecting mothers in rural Martin County who face barriers to accessing maternity care. Mom Mobile, launched by the Martin County Healthy Start Coalition, delivers prenatal care and support directly to pregnant women and their families in underserved communities. The program has proven so successful that it has expanded to neighboring Okeechobee County, where the need for such services is equally critical.

Twenty-year-old Evelyn Allen discovered Mom Mobile after struggling to find affordable prenatal care options. Allen explained that available resources either required out-of-pocket payments or had expectations she could not meet. When she first learned she was pregnant while trying to improve her circumstances, she felt terrified and unsure where to turn. The discovery of Mom Mobile changed her experience significantly. According to Allen, "I couldn't find any resources and the resources I did find you have to come out of pocket for it, or they would expect you to do more and you can't." She added that it was difficult to find places willing to provide help without barriers.

The expansion to Okeechobee County came after Andrea Medellin with the Okeechobee Healthy Start Coalition witnessed the program's impact and recognized her community had the same urgent need. Okeechobee County has no hospitals that deliver babies, forcing pregnant women to travel to Fort Pierce or Highlands County depending on their location. The 38-foot mobile clinic is now stationed at the public library on West 16th Street every Tuesday, offering hour-long appointments designed specifically to provide quality care for high-risk and high-need mothers. Medellin explained the intentional approach: "This bus looks like an hour-long visit for moms. It's intentional, it's specifically set not to serve more but to serve quality for our high-risk and need moms."

The demand for the service became clear immediately upon arrival in Okeechobee. During the first three days of operation, fifteen women received care, and appointment requests have continued to come in. Allen appreciates the ongoing support from nursing staff with the Okeechobee Healthy Start Coalition, who assured her she could always call with concerns. Having professional support throughout her pregnancy journey has made a significant difference for Allen. She describes the Mom Mobile program as a blessing, reflecting on how the accessible, judgment-free care has transformed her experience during a time when she felt vulnerable and uncertain.

cards.headline: Jupiter and Venus make closest approach visible after sunset tonight
cards.teaser: Two of the brightest planets will make their closest approach tonight in the twilight sky in what astronomers call a cosmic kiss.
cards.body:
Two of the brightest planets will make their closest approach tonight in the twilight sky. Jupiter and Venus have been creeping closer together and will cross paths in the west northwest sky. Just after the 8:14 p.m. sunset, Venus will appear followed by Jupiter, which is not as bright. The pair will make their closest approach about 1.5 degrees apart, appearing as wide as a pinky held at arm's distance. This event is sometimes referred to as a "cosmic kiss."

Mercury will also appear low on the horizon during the event. The planets will set before 11 p.m. After tonight, Venus will surpass Jupiter and appear farther west in the sky.

cards.headline: 6.1 magnitude earthquake off Cuba felt across Florida from Miami to Jacksonville
cards.teaser: A 6.1 magnitude earthquake off the west-northwest coast of Cuba prompted building evacuations in Miami and was felt as far north as Jacksonville on Tuesday.
cards.body:
A 6.1 magnitude earthquake off the west-northwest coast of Cuba prompted evacuations of several buildings across Miami on Tuesday and was felt as far north as Jacksonville. Students at Fusion Academy were among those evacuated, with those on upper floors reporting they felt the quake more intensely. Student Maria Torrado said the evacuation announcement was urgent, with staff emphasizing it was not a drill. "The people that are in the top floors, which they said that they felt it even more than we did," Torrado said of the experience.

Not all evacuees felt the earthquake. Students at the Swatch Watchmaking School were evacuated but initially had no idea why. Student Jack Hodapp said many in the break room did not feel any shaking. Streets near affected buildings were temporarily blocked off as the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office set up a command center. Those evacuated were allowed back inside shortly after. The National Weather Service confirmed there is no tsunami risk from the earthquake. No injuries have been reported.

cards.headline: DAS Beer Garden in Jupiter plans World Cup street party with free beer for USA goals
cards.teaser: DAS Beer Garden in Jupiter is preparing for the FIFA World Cup with free beer for every Team USA goal and a street party planned for the final match.
cards.body:
DAS Beer Garden in Jupiter is preparing for the FIFA World Cup by offering fans free beer for every Team USA goal scored and planning a street party for the final match. Co-owner Alex Marquez said the World Cup brings an energy unlike any other sporting event. "When the World Cup starts, it's just different. You can just see the vibe changes, everybody gets really into it," Marquez said. He explained that the tournament carries deeper meaning for fans than typical matches. "Now it's your country. It's your blood, it's your heritage," Marquez said. Marquez also noted that soccer's lower-scoring nature contributes to the excitement. "Sometimes it's less scoring. But a lot of people believe that's a bad thing. I think that's a good thing because the expectation of that score builds up so much that when that happens, that's when you see people not pretending to lose their minds, but really losing their minds," he said.

The tavern at 1203 Town Center Drive, Suite 116 in Jupiter will host morning watch parties featuring donuts. Soccer fan Jason Pitman said he plans to be a regular at the bar during the tournament. "One of those people at 9 a.m. eating those donuts that Alex brings in," Pitman said. He expressed optimism about Team USA's prospects, saying "I think we're talented. I think it's just a matter of trying to put that talent together." For the World Cup Final, DAS Beer Garden plans to shut down Town Center Drive and set up a large television screen across the street for an outdoor street party.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County implements 45-day anchoring limits in Indian River Lagoon and Fort Pierce Harbor
hero.body:
St. Lucie County established new anchoring restrictions for boaters in the Indian River Lagoon and Fort Pierce Harbor near the South Causeway Bridge, effective June 1. Under the new rules, boaters cannot anchor a vessel for more than 45 consecutive days within any six-month period in designated anchoring limitation areas. Anyone anchoring in these zones must leave all anchoring limitation areas for at least 24 hours before returning.

County officials say the restrictions directly address the problem of abandoned vessels accumulating in these waterways. According to Erick Gill with St. Lucie County, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission collected approximately two dozen derelict vessels from the area during the previous year. Gill explained that the new anchoring limits will improve navigation by keeping the waterways clear and accessible for other boats. "We need to make sure that highway for vessels is clear and free for other vessels to come and go," Gill said.

Environmental protection played a major role in the decision to implement these restrictions. James Beams with St. Lucie County Port, Inlet and Beaches previously warned that abandoned vessels sitting in the water for extended periods could harm water quality. These deteriorating vessels pose significant environmental risks because they contain diesel tanks, oil tanks, and holding tanks that can leak or rupture. Gill stated that the new anchoring limits will help prevent these pollutants from contaminating the water. The Indian River Lagoon supports an extraordinarily diverse ecosystem, with over 4,000 species of animals, plants, and birds living there. Gill emphasized the county's commitment to protecting this sensitive environment from contamination.

St. Lucie County residents and boaters who want more information about the anchor limitation areas can access a site map through the county. The restrictions represent an effort to balance the needs of the boating community with environmental protection and water quality concerns in one of Florida's most ecologically important waterways.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County implements 45-day anchoring limits in Indian River Lagoon to combat abandoned vessels
hero.body:

The regulations create anchor limitation areas where boat owners cannot keep vessels anchored for more than 45 consecutive days within any six-month period. Anyone wishing to anchor longer must leave all designated anchoring limitation areas for at least 24 hours before returning.

The county took this action in response to a growing problem with abandoned vessels in local waterways. During the previous year, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission removed approximately two dozen derelict vessels from the area. According to Erick Gill with St. Lucie County, these restrictions will improve navigation in the waterways. "We need to make sure that highway for vessels is clear and free for other vessels to come and go," Gill said. The new rules aim to keep channels open and accessible for legitimate boating traffic.

Abandoned vessels pose significant environmental risks to the lagoon's ecosystem. James Beams with St. Lucie County Port, Inlet and Beaches explained that when vessels remain in the water for extended periods, they threaten water quality. Abandoned boats contain diesel tanks, oil tanks, and holding tanks that can leak pollutants into the surrounding water. The Indian River Lagoon supports an exceptionally diverse ecosystem with over 4,000 species of animals, plants, and birds. Gill stressed the importance of protecting this valuable natural resource.
